newsitem.title: UK: Crude tender beats effect of Med refinery run cuts.
newsitem.headline: Crude tender beats effect of Med refinery run cuts.

text.p: A Turkish tender for 300,000 tonnes of crude oil has helped keep Russian Urals firm, despite the negative effect on demand of extensive run cuts in the Mediterranean, traders said.
The tender by state oil company Tupras, announced on Monday and due to close by the end of the week, had badly unsettled the market, they added.
Doubt existed that Tupras would follow through with the large tender, given the scarcity of Urals barrels and the high prices they were likely to be offered.

"There are so few people able to offer Urals that the Turks may have to go for different grades or postpone their tender when they see the prices they'll be quoted," said one seller. "That's put a lot of uncertainty into the market."
Strong numbers have already been reported in the wake of the tender.
Traders were astounded by the 67 cents below dated Brent reportedly paid for a July 11-13 loading Urals on Monday.
One sceptical refinery described it as "a very solid number," particularly as at the same time he was offered a cargo from the same date range at -80 cents a barrel.
"It was done at a lot higher than I expected," said another trader.
Despite the continued absence of Iraqi barrels, the dampening effect of run cuts on demand should have begun to help Urals prices drift down, traders said.
"An amount like 300,000 tonnes is a lot to take out of a market that was balanced to over-supplied," said one.

Urals prices have ridden high since Iraq's last shipment of crude, under the first phase of its oil-for-food deal with the U.N., in late May, recovering from a low of around $1.40 below dated Brent to a high of close to -55 cents.
Bureaucratic and political delays have made crude exports from Iraq under the accord's second term unlikely before August.
High Urals prices have crucified profit margins for refinery operators in the Mediterranean area recently, leading several to cut crude throughput.
ERG cut throughput at its 230,000 barrels per day (bpd) plant in Sicily by 15-20 percent at the end of last week, said traders familiar with the refinery's workings.
"They need nothing at the moment, margins are just so poor," one trader said. "Nobody has any incentive to buy."
Saras cut back at their 320,000 bpd plant by 10 percent a week ago and had no immediate plans to resume full throughput, trade sources said.
British Petroleum was reported to be considering an imminent cut of 20 percent, or some 40,000 bpd, at its plant at Lavera in southern France, because of poor margins, sources said.
A simple hydroskimming unit running Russian Urals in the Med was losing 57 cents on every barrel processed this week, according to Reuters data using standard product yields.
